extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology; literary critics; advanced creative writers
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical guidelines for identifying and evaluating modes of focalization, the narrating instance (voice), and the temporal relation between narrating and story in fictional narrative, with Proustian examples and technical vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal focalization / focalization through the hero
rubrics_metrics.description: When the narrating is contemporaneous with the story (interior monologue, journal, correspondence), internal focalization on the narrator amounts to focalization on the hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat narrating that is contemporaneous with events as equivalent to the hero's point of view; respect the hero's ignorance and reconstruct the evolution of his thought from his perspective (examples: interior monologue, epistolary novel; reference to Proust's handling of Marcel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of nonintervention (narrator restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator may forbid himself from giving premature signs or indiscreet encouragement, in order to respect the hero's ignorance (e.g., Proust delaying explanations of the madeleine experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid premature explanation from the narrating voice; withholding information can be a deliberate technique to preserve suspense or subjectivity. Note risk: such restraint can produce lasting misunderstandings between narrator and reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of single-protagonist point of view to render others mysterious ('creature in flight')
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically adopting the 'point of view' of one protagonist permits an author to leave the feelings of the other nearly in shadow and construct for that other a mysterious, ambiguous personality (Proust's 'creature in flight').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal focalization can deliberately limit knowledge about other characters to emphasize subjectivity (illustrated by amorous relationships in Proust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modalizing locutions as focalization markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of words like perhaps, as if, seem, appear allows the narrator to hypothesize what cannot be asserted without stepping outside internal focalization; these are 'the alibis of the novelist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such modalizing expressions as indicators of the narrator's (or hero's) uncertainty and as devices that permit indirect comment while remaining within focalization; multiplicity of hypotheses weakens claims and signals insolubility rather than definitive explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous perceptual restriction in focalized description
rubrics_metrics.description: Proustian descriptions are rigorously focalized: their 'duration' never exceeds that of real contemplation, and their content never exceeds what is actually perceived by the contemplator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating descriptive passages, check that content and temporal extent are limited to what the perceiving character could have seen/heard; note deliberate partial perceptions (e.g., scenes seen through slanting bars, windows) and narrative respect for sensory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paralipsis (hyperrestriction / withholding)
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of hyperrestriction of field where events or knowledge are deliberately left out (paralipsis), sometimes disclosed later by the narrator and known to readers only through later revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize paralipsis as an intentional withholding strategy distinct from simple omission; its existence may only be revealed by later narrator intervention and must be contextualized within the narrative system (not automatically a violation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between narrator's knowledge and novelist omniscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance notices, prolepses, and phrases like 'I have learned since...' belong to the narrator's subsequent knowledge and are legitimate in autobiographical or first-person framed narratives; they are not necessarily signs of the novelist's omniscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing information to an 'omniscient novelist,' first ask whether the narrator (as a narrating instance) plausibly could have obtained the information later; attribute to 'novelist' only what cannot reasonably be ascribed to the narrator's knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for true omniscience (paralepsis irreducible to narrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the narrative reports, on the spot and with no plausible way station, the private thoughts of other characters (e.g., Bergotte's last thoughts), this irreducibility to narrator's information must be attributed to an omniscient novelist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use textual coherence and narrative tonality (not material impossibility alone) to judge whether an instance is a genuine transgression into omniscience; identify passages that give the impression of immediate reporting without plausible source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polymodality / coexistence of multiple focalization modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The text may operate in three modes at once—focalization through the hero, focalization through the narrator, and zero-focalization/omniscience—and pass among them freely; this 'polymodality' is distinct from classical omniscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the narrative systematically shifts among modes and whether these shifts form an integrated practice rather than sporadic lapses; consider polytonal/polymodal analogy: multiple coexisting codes rather than single dominant code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrating instance (voice) distinct from author
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'I' of narration (narrating instance) is identifiable only by reference to the enunciating situation and is not identical with the real author; narrating situation can differ from the act of writing and may change within a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate narrator, narratee/receiver, and author; assess textual traces of the narrating situation (who tells, when, and in what circumstances) and track any shifts of narrating instance across embedded or multi-voiced narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal position of narrating relative to story (types of narrating)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief temporal determination of the narrating instance is its position relative to the story: subsequent (classical past-tense), prior (predictive/future-oriented), simultaneous (present-tense contemporaneous), or interpolated (inserted between moments of action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify narrations by temporal relation to the story; assess effects of each type on narrative meaning and modality (e.g., predictive narratives, live present narratives, journal/letter forms which approximate simultaneity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal distance / elapsed time between event and narrating
rubrics_metrics.description: How much time elapses between the events told and the narrating moment is a decisive element in the narrative's significance (e.g., 'Many years have passed since that night').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate narrative significance by measuring narrating distance; long retrospective intervals, recent recountings, or interpolated commentaries change the interpretive frame and authority of the narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative irrelevance of narrating place (spatial location)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike time, the narrating place (where the story is told) is rarely specified and almost never relevant, except in second-degree narratings where diegetic context makes it salient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume narrating place is always meaningful; consider it only when diegetic cues or the narrating situation (e.g., a prison, hospital) make location a decisive interpretive factor.
